title: NSFOCUS: new VeilDHT botnet spreads to Linux servers and IoT devices
date_note: NSFOCUS's post gives only its publication day; the infection counts it cites are for 16 to 26 October 2026.
geo_basis: country named by the source for the infections (mainland China)
summary: NSFOCUS's risk alert describes VeilDHT, a previously unseen botnet it says mainly targets Linux servers and IoT devices. NSFOCUS says it spreads by exploiting flaws including CVE-2024-3912 (ASUS routers) and CVE-2021-35394 (Realtek Jungle SDK), can run DDoS attacks and commands, and hides a backup C2 channel in a public P2P network. CNCERT observed as many as 15,805 active bots in a single day, with a cumulative total of 40,467 infected devices.
plain: Researchers at NSFOCUS describe a new hidden botnet that infects Linux servers and internet-connected devices such as routers, and can launch DDoS attacks and run commands on them.
exec: NSFOCUS says the new botnet, with as many as 15,805 active bots in a single day, targets Linux servers and IoT devices.
action: NSFOCUS advises keeping an up-to-date asset inventory, patching known vulnerabilities including IoT firmware, monitoring DNS and IP activity tied to its IOCs, and isolating and remediating any infected host.

evidence.quote: as many as 15,805 active bots in a single day, with a cumulative total of 40,467 infected devices

validation.note: Only NSFOCUS's own post was read; Security Boulevard republishes it, so it is one publisher and was not read separately.

key_findings: NSFOCUS describes VeilDHT as a highly stealthy, previously unseen botnet primarily targeting Linux servers and IoT devices.
It mainly spreads by exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-3912 (ASUS routers) and CVE-2021-35394 (Realtek Jungle SDK).
It can run DDoS attacks, execute commands, open reverse shells and act as a reverse proxy.
Its C2 address is obtained through spoofed-IP DNS responses and DHT traffic blending.
CNCERT observed as many as 15,805 active bots in a single day, with a cumulative total of 40,467 infected devices, between 16 and 26 October 2026.
recommendations: Keep an up-to-date asset inventory and patch vulnerabilities, including IoT firmware.
Monitor DNS and IP activity tied to the listed IOCs and block anomalies.
If infected, verify the extent and entry point, isolate and remediate the host, and report to local authorities.
